canonicalExplanation.summary: How you pass a parameter tells callers what happens to their data. **By value** (`int x`, `std::string s`): the function gets its own copy; ideal for small types, and for things it will **keep** (take by value, then `std::move` into storage). **By const reference** (`const std::string& s`): borrow to **read** without copying; the usual choice for large inputs. **By reference** (`std::string& s`): the function will **modify the caller's object**. **By pointer** (`T*`): like a reference but may be **null**, meaning "optional". Smart pointers express **ownership** (next module). There's no single "fastest" form: choose by intent.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner writes every parameter as `const std::string&`, including `void set_name(const std::string& n) { name_ = n; }`. Callers passing temporaries like `set_name(first + " " + last)` pay for a copy that could have been a cheap move. A setter takes std::string by value and moves it into storage, supporting both lvalues and rvalues with one ownership-taking interface. In this lesson you'll choose and justify parameter forms for scalar and class-type values.

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **Loops and range iteration**, **Calls, parameters and returns** and **Function contracts and return values** (ownership and side effects).

sections.heading: The rule: the parameter form states the intent
Not always const&

includes: Choose value, const reference, reference, pointer or sink-by-value parameters by intent.
Use std::move to transfer a by-value parameter into storage.

outcomes: Choose and justify parameter forms for scalar and class-type values.

examples.title: A setter that takes by value and moves
examples.situation: A setter takes std::string by value and moves it into storage, supporting both lvalues and rvalues with one ownership-taking interface.
walkthrough: **A setter takes std::string by value:** set_name(std::string n).
**Moves it into storage:** name_ = std::move(n) transfers the buffer instead of copying it again.
**Supporting both lvalues and rvalues with one ownership-taking interface:** set_name(saved) copies once, set_name(first + " " + last) will copy nothing.
examples.result: One setter handles every caller efficiently, and its signature says "I keep this".

examples.title: The accidental copy loop
examples.situation: `int count_long(std::vector<std::string> words)` is called in a hot loop with a 50,000-word vector.
walkthrough: Each call copies the whole vector.
The function only reads, so use const std::vector<std::string>&.
Inside, loop with const auto& too.
examples.result: The function reads the words with no copying at all.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: Passing every object by const reference is always fastest and always communicates the correct ownership contract.
misconceptions.correction: const& is right for reading large objects, but small types are cheaper by value, and functions that keep a copy are better as by-value-then-move. The form should match the intent.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, what did set_name(const std::string&) cost callers passing temporaries?

analogy.example: Parameter forms are like **ways to share a document**. By value: **give a photocopy**. const&: **let them read over your shoulder**. &: **hand them your pen and the original**. Pointer: **"here's the original, if I have one"**. By-value-then-move: **"give me a copy to keep, or the original if you're done with it"**.
usefulFor: remembering copy, look, edit, maybe, keep
match the form to the intent
limitations: Photocopies of a sticky note are free; copying ints is too.
Reading over a shoulder requires the owner to stay (lifetime).

nearTransfer.prompt: Choose and justify the parameter form for: a function printing a long report string, one doubling every element of a vector in place, one taking an age, one storing a label in an object, and one that may receive no logger.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a small Playlist class with add(std::string title), a const& accessor, a function that renames all titles in place, and a statistics function taking const Playlist&. Count copies with a custom type that prints on copy and move, and confirm no unnecessary copies.
scaffold: A struct with noisy copy and move constructors.
Try both lvalue and temporary arguments.

remediation.explanation: For each parameter ask: **will the function read, modify, keep, or maybe-receive it?** Then pick const&, &, by-value-and-move, or pointer. Small types: just by value.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The accidental copy loop".

recap.summary: To choose parameter forms, pass small types by value, large read-only inputs by const reference, objects to modify by reference, optional ones by pointer, and values the function will keep by value followed by std::move, so each signature communicates copying, borrowing, mutation and ownership.
